newsitem.title: USA: Dollar argues against March Fed rate hike - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Dollar argues against March Fed rate hike - Merrill.

text.p: The likelihood that the dollar would rally sharply if the Federal Reserve raises interest rates this month offers a strong argument in favor of waiting, according to a Merrill Lynch economist.

Specifically, a spike in dollar/mark could pressure the Bundesbank to follow a Fed rate hike with one of its own at a time when the struggling German economy can ill afford it, said John Praveen, Merrill international economist.
Thus far in 1997 the dollar has risen more than 10 percent versus the mark, buoyed by relatively strong U.S. economic readings and the growing chorus of predictions of higher official interest rates.
But the mark's slide threatens to boost German inflation and many Bundesbank officials have repeatedly called for an end to the dollar's rally.
"If the dollar rises at a very accelerated pace, then there is a risk of accelerated (German) inflation and to counter that risk, the Bundesbank would have to raise rates," Praveen said.
Most foreign exchange experts see the dollar grinding higher in 1997, with some calling for a dollar/mark rate near 2.00, up from roughly 1.70 now.
A gradual dollar rise would bring only modest increases in prices of imported goods to Germany, notably commodities, which are priced in dollars, Merrill said.
But a Fed rate hike at the March 25 Federal Open Market Committee meeting might trigger sharp dollar gains immediately, Praveen cautioned.

Several Fed officials have recently cited the dollar's strength as a disinflationary force and some Fed alumni said it might marginally reduce any rate hike fever at the Fed.
But when push comes to shove, Chariman Alan Greenspan and his Fed colleagues will act to stop U.S. inflation regardless of the impact in Europe, Fed-watchers said.
"I think the dollar will be one of several constraints that will inhibit them, but will it as such prevent them from going? No," said Preston Martin, a former Fed vice chairman.

The U.S. jobless rate has held at or below 5.5 percent since late 1995. And while wage gains have stayed mystifyingly low, many economists see modest inflation pressures building, which argues for higher U.S. interest rates.
Martin, now chairman at HomeVest Financial Services, said he sees an even-money bet on the prospects for a rate hike at the March 25 FOMC meeting.
The latest Reuters poll showed 17 of 44 analysts predicting a rate hike at that meeting, with 34 of 44 calling for higher rates by the May 20 meeting.
The Fed has held its overnight interbank lending rate target, the federal funds rate, at 5.25 percent since January 31, 1996.
Economists note the dollar's rise also has positive implications for Europe. Notably, a rising dollar makes U.S. goods less competitive and bolsters exports to the United States.
With much of Europe suffering double-digit unemployment rates, many European policy-makers have welcomed the dollar's rise as a much-needed economic boost.
Thus, while a Fed rate hike and a higher dollar might raise some import prices in Europe, the stimulatory benefit outweighs the inflation risk, said former Fed Governor Robert Heller.
"It would help the European economies by making American goods more expensive. A Fed rate hike would be tolerable for the Europeans," said Heller.
The strength of the dollar is the strongest current argument against a Fed tightening at the March FOMC, Heller added.
But given the tight labor market and the steady pace of U.S. economic growth, Heller agrees with Martin that the probability of a rate hike at the upcoming meeting is about 50 percent.
